## 13. Key terms

Terms taught in this Note come first; linked terms are recaps, taught in the Note the link opens.

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Global planner (G-2910) | The planner that finds a route over the whole map, from the robot to its goal, and runs rarely, such as A\* on a room's grid or a road network; its route, the global plan, guides the local planner but has no timing and knows only the map. |
| Behavioural layer (behavioural decision making) (G-2912) | The level of planning between route planning and motion planning that decides which task the vehicle carries out now, such as following the lane, stopping at a line or giving way, from the route and what it perceives; the motion planner then plans that task. |
| Local planner (G-2911) | The planner that turns the next few metres or seconds of the global plan into a timed trajectory within the robot's limits and around obstacles its sensors see, solving again many times a second, such as TEB at 10 Hz over 1.5 m; it handles what the global plan cannot. |
| Local goal (virtual goal) (G-2929) | The pose on the global plan at the end of the local planner's window, facing along the plan, which the local planner plans to reach; it moves along the plan with the robot, and becomes the real goal when that comes within reach. |
| Warm start (G-2914) | Starting a solver from an earlier answer, such as the last cycle's trajectory or a planner's path, instead of from scratch; each solve then only corrects a nearby answer, and the starting point also decides which local minimum it reaches. |
| Receding horizon (G-2913) | Planning over a window of fixed length that starts at the robot's current state, applying only the first part of the plan, then planning again from the new state, so the window slides forward with the robot; it lets a planner take in new obstacles and correct errors every cycle. |
| Trajectory (G-2886) | The state of a robot at every moment of a time interval, together with the controls that produce it, such as a local planner's band of poses with times; unlike a path, it says when the robot is where and how fast it moves. |
| Decision variables (G-2915) | The numbers an optimisation is free to choose, such as the poses and time steps of a band or the controls at each interval; the solver changes them to lower the cost while the constraints hold. |
| Trajectory optimisation (G-2887) | Choosing the numbers that describe a trajectory to make a cost such as the time or the effort as small as possible while the motion rules, the start and the end, the limits and the clearance from obstacles hold; it computes one good trajectory where a rule for every state would be far too large. |
| Hard constraint (G-2916) | A constraint the answer must meet exactly, so no answer that breaks it is accepted, such as a wheel speed that may never pass 0.6 m/s; it holds whatever it costs. |
| Soft constraint (penalty) (G-2917) | A constraint replaced by an extra cost that is 0 while it holds and grows with how far it is broken, such as a weighted squared excess over a speed limit; the problem then has no constraints and is easy to solve, but the answer may break the limit a little when that lowers the total cost. |
| Second difference (G-2918) | For three neighbouring points of a path, the two outer points minus twice the middle one, $p_{k-1} - 2p_k + p_{k+1}$; it is zero on a straight, evenly spaced stretch and large where the path bends, so its square measures how unsmooth the path is. |
| Elastic band (G-2919) | A path treated as a chain of points that a cost pulls straight, like a stretched rubber band, while bounds or obstacles hold it in place, and optimised; Autoware's smoother of this kind minimises squared second differences with small sideways moves as a quadratic program. |
| Timed elastic band (TEB) (G-2920) | A trajectory written as a list of poses with the time between neighbours, optimised for the least total time while penalties keep the motion rule, the speed and acceleration limits and the clearance from obstacles; a ROS and Nav2 local planner that solves it again every cycle from its last answer. |
| Levenberg–Marquardt method (G-2921) | A solver for sums of squares that takes Gauss–Newton steps, jumping to the lowest point of a bowl built from straight-line guesses of each term, blended with a small step downhill that grows when a step fails and shrinks when it succeeds; it converges fast near the answer and safely far from it. |
| Transcription (G-2888) | Turning a trajectory optimisation problem, whose unknowns are functions of time, into one whose unknowns are a finite list of numbers, such as a band's 10 poses and the 9 time steps between them, 39 numbers, so that an optimiser can search over them. |
| Direct collocation (G-2893) | Transcription in which the states and controls at a row of points in time are all unknowns and the motion rules are equations between neighbouring points; nothing is simulated, so limits along the way are easy to add. |
| Knot point (collocation point) (G-2895) | One of the points in time at which collocation keeps the state and controls as unknowns, such as 31 points 0.206 s apart over a 6.18 s drive; more knot points make the solution more accurate. |
| Collocation constraint (trapezoidal) (G-2894) | The equation that ties neighbouring knot points through the motion rules; in trapezoidal collocation the change in state equals the time step times the average of the rates at the two points, $x_{k+1} - x_k = \frac{h}{2}(f_k + f_{k+1})$, so a simulation is not needed. |
| Finite-difference collocation (G-2923) | Direct collocation in which the motion rules are written as differences between neighbouring points, such as a speed equal to the distance between two poses over the time between them; TEB is derived this way. |
| Piecewise-jerk optimisation (G-2924) | A quadratic program that keeps a quantity, its slope and its second slope at stations as unknowns and holds the third slope (the jerk) constant between neighbours, so neighbours are tied by exact equations; Apollo plans a car's sideways path and its speed this way. |
| Homotopy class (G-2922) | A set of paths with the same start and goal that can be bent into one another without crossing an obstacle, such as all paths passing a person on the left; an optimiser never leaves the class it starts in, so a search must pick the class. |
| OSQP (G-2926) | A solver for quadratic programs, a squared cost with linear bounds, that can start from its last answer; Autoware's smoothers and Apollo's path and speed optimisers use it every planning cycle. |
| g2o (G-2927) | A library that solves sparse least-squares problems written as a graph, each term joining a few variables, with Gauss–Newton or Levenberg–Marquardt steps; TEB solves its band with it. |
| IPOPT (G-2928) | A solver for general optimisation problems with curved costs and constraints; one of Apollo's parking optimisers and some MPC planners use it. |
| Path–speed decomposition (path then speed) (G-2925) | Planning a trajectory in two steps, first the shape of the path and then the speed profile along that fixed path, so each step is a smaller, simpler problem; Autoware and Apollo plan this way. |
| [Route planning (mission planning)](../../../../RO/navigation/06-grid-sampling-and-car-like-planning/RO-057-route-planning-on-road-graphs/RO-057-route-planning-on-road-graphs.md#2-why-route-planning-is-its-own-level) (G-2870) | Finding the best way from where a vehicle is to its destination on a map of the road network, by travel time or by distance, such as the 492.8 s route across the Chicago map; the top level of planning, which picks the roads and lanes and leaves the motion to the levels below. |
| [State $x_t$](../../../../RO/localization/02-bayes-filters/RO-007-why-a-robot-is-never-sure/RO-007-why-a-robot-is-never-sure.md#41-state-from-one-number-to-many) (G-2314) | The quantities a robot keeps track of at time $t$ because they decide what happens next, such as its pose, its speeds and moving things around it; it is what localization and filtering estimate. |
| [Control input $u$](../../../../RO/control/01-robot-models/RO-001-pose-and-differential-drive/RO-001-pose-and-differential-drive.md#52-the-kinematic-model) (G-2298) | The numbers we choose to drive a robot, such as $u = (v, \omega)$; the model turns them into motion. |
| [Kinematic model](../../../../RO/control/01-robot-models/RO-001-pose-and-differential-drive/RO-001-pose-and-differential-drive.md#52-the-kinematic-model) (G-2297) | Equations that give how a robot's configuration changes from its speed inputs alone, ignoring masses and forces, such as $\dot{x} = v\cos\theta$, $\dot{y} = v\sin\theta$, $\dot{\theta} = \omega$; used to predict motion at low speed. |
| [Constraint](../../../../ML/07-classification/ML-087-svm-maths/ML-087-svm-maths.md#42-one-constraint-for-both-classes) (G-456) | A condition the solution must satisfy; in SVM, $y_i (w^T x_i + b) \geq 1$ for every training point. |
| [Policy](../../../../ML/01-foundations/ML-003-types-of-ml/ML-003-types-of-ml.md#51-agent-environment-policy-and-reward) (G-1512) | The agent's rules for which action to take. |
| [Path smoothing](../../../../RO/navigation/06-grid-sampling-and-car-like-planning/RO-055-hybrid-a-star-and-path-smoothing/RO-055-hybrid-a-star-and-path-smoothing.md#51-the-smoothing-rule) (G-2842) | Moving the points of a found path, sweep after sweep, a little towards their found places and a little towards their neighbours, $y_i \leftarrow y_i + \alpha(x_i - y_i) + \beta(y_{i+1} + y_{i-1} - 2y_i)$; it rounds corners and removes needless steering, but on its own it knows nothing of obstacles, the turning circle or the goal heading. |
| [Unit vector](../../../../ML/05-dimensionality/ML-047-pca-step-by-step/ML-047-pca-step-by-step.md#21-projecting-one-point) (G-2048) | A vector of length 1, used to describe a direction. |
| [Dot product](../../../../MA/05-linear-algebra/MA-050-dot-product-and-cosine-similarity/MA-050-dot-product-and-cosine-similarity.md#3-computing-the-dot-product) (G-634) | Multiplying two vectors entry by entry and adding the products, $u^{\mathsf T}x$, which gives one number. It is large when the vectors point the same way, so it measures similarity and gives projections. |
| [Matrix](../../../../ML/01-foundations/ML-010-tensors/ML-010-tensors.md#2-what-a-tensor-is) (G-1180) | A table of numbers in rows and columns (a 2D tensor); it can hold a dataset (one row per observation), and multiplying a vector by it transforms the vector. |
| [Quadratic program](../../../../MA/07-optimisation/MA-068-linear-and-quadratic-programming/MA-068-linear-and-quadratic-programming.md#1-overview) (G-1598) | A problem of finding the lowest point of a bowl-shaped function with squared terms (a convex quadratic) while meeting limits written as linear inequalities (constraints). |
| [Nonholonomic constraint](../../../../RO/control/01-robot-models/RO-001-pose-and-differential-drive/RO-001-pose-and-differential-drive.md#62-can-the-robot-still-get-everywhere) (G-2302) | A rule on velocities that does not follow from any equation on the pose, such as a wheel that cannot slide sideways; it limits which way a robot can move at each moment but not which poses it can reach. |
| [Ordinary least squares (OLS, least squares)](../../../../ML/06-regression/ML-050-linear-regression-maths/ML-050-linear-regression-maths.md#2-two-ways-to-find-m-and-b) (G-1406) | The way linear regression finds its line with one formula (a closed-form method): the line with the smallest sum of squared errors. |
| [Jacobian](../../../../MA/06-calculus/MA-063-jacobian-and-matrix-gradients/MA-063-jacobian-and-matrix-gradients.md#42-the-formula-every-partial-derivative-in-one-grid) (G-980) | The table (matrix) of all first partial derivatives of a function with several inputs and outputs, one row per output and one column per input, $J_{ij} = \partial f_i/\partial x_j$; it shows how every output changes with every input near a point. |
| [Sparse](../../../../DL/04-cnn/DL-052-visualizing-cnn/DL-052-visualizing-cnn.md#7-feature-maps-get-sparser-with-depth) (G-1846) | Mostly made of zeros, such as a feature map whose values are almost all 0, or a model whose coefficients are mostly exactly 0. |
| [Local minimum](../../../../ML/06-regression/ML-056-gradient-descent/ML-056-gradient-descent.md#8-the-shape-of-the-loss-function-matters) (G-1110) | A point lower than everything around it, but not the lowest overall. |
| [OMPL (Open Motion Planning Library)](../../../../RO/navigation/06-grid-sampling-and-car-like-planning/RO-053-manipulation-planning/RO-053-manipulation-planning.md#5-the-software-moveit-and-ompl) (G-2814) | A library of sampling-based planners, such as PRM and RRT, that by design has no collision checker or robot model, so it can be joined to any; MoveIt uses it by default. |
